Our mission is to turn frontier intelligence into real results for every business. We charge for results, not access.
Tenex was founded in New York City in 2025. We are roughly 50 people today and our end-of-year target is 150. We ship production AI for Fortune 500 clients, and one in three of our engineers has founded a company. Our engineers work directly with C-suite leaders to find where AI can change their business, and then build the custom systems that make it work in production at the boundary of what is possible.
The Associate Forward Deployed Engineer is how that happens. It is not a support role and not a services role. It is the role.
Why the work is hard
We now have superintelligence on demand, but model capabilities are advancing faster than companies can adapt, so most of that value goes untapped. The hard part starts after the model. Building reliable systems around frontier models means connecting fragmented data, rethinking workflows from first principles, building evaluations and controls, and adapting as fast as the frontier labs ship.
The most important work now happens at the edge, where AI meets real world conditions. That is the only place we work.
What You Will Do
You own the outcome. You work with the customer, frame the problem, choose the architecture, build the system, ship it, and stay accountable for what happens in production:
Discover. You embed inside a real business, learn how it makes money, and find where AI would create real value rather than a demo.
Decide. You turn ambiguity into a product direction and a technical plan, and you defend both when someone senior disagrees.
Build. You ship the system, not a disconnected piece of it, and you make the build-versus-buy and architecture calls yourself.
Own. You measure what happens in production and keep improving it after the merge.
At this level you own a workstream outright. You decide what gets built and in what order, you are the technical voice the client hears on that work, and when the scope turns out to be wrong you are the one who says so and re-cuts it. You are closer to a founder inside an engagement than a contributor on an assembly line.
The platform you help build
Tenex is rebuilding the software development lifecycle around coding agents. The goal is a software factory that carries work from a business problem to a production system with increasing agent autonomy, where planning, architecture, implementation, testing, review, and delivery become one connected system rather than a series of handoffs.
You will learn how to structure work for agents, engineer durable context, evaluate outputs, and decide where deterministic software and human judgment remain in control. The system is early, it is already used by everyone here, and it provides real leverage today. Engineers who join now will help decide how it works.
This matters beyond your own engagement. Every engagement produces reusable agent systems, evals, and tools that make the next one faster, so the work you do compounds instead of ending when the client signs off.
The work itself
Every engagement changes the problem. Each one brings a different industry, architecture, and set of technical constraints, across finance, software companies, media, industrials, energy, logistics, professional sports teams, healthcare, consumer packaged goods, real estate, and market research. That exposure keeps the work interesting and forces you to learn faster than you have anywhere else.
Recent work includes the operating system a private equity firm with $115 billion under management runs on, AI verification of every in-store sampling station for a national retailer with 70,000 field staff, and camera systems across thousands of retail stores that catch theft, manage queues, and track inventory on the floor.
Some of what we hit has no established solution yet, including agent orchestration, evaluation, memory, and long-running execution. You will work at the boundary between what the newest models appear capable of and what can actually be made reliable in production.
Growth
Tenex has more demand than capacity. New engagements, products, and teams create a constant need for people who can own larger problems, so nobody here waits for a seat above them to open. Engineers who deliver are trusted with broader technical decisions, more important client relationships, and greater responsibility across the company.
One year here is worth several years elsewhere in engineering, product, customer, and leadership growth, because the mechanism is the work itself rather than a development program.
Who We Look For
We are a people business. The engineers we put in front of clients are the product, so hiring is the highest-stakes decision we make each week. The pattern we bet on is the high-slope generalist, meaning a strong engineer who has shipped real software, moved hard into AI, and improves faster than their peers.
At this level, you are likely one or two years into your career, though we care much more about what you have built than how long you have been building. We look for a few specific things:
You have shipped production software that real people depended on, whether at a job, at your own company, or on something you built alone.
You have built something real with LLMs and can explain honestly where it worked and where it did not.
You get productive in an unfamiliar domain within days, because every engagement asks you to.
You can explain a technical decision to a CEO as clearly as you can to another engineer.
You use AI in your own work every day and have opinions about how to do it well.
The environment
Tenex is intense by design. We work together in Manhattan five days a week, the pace is fast, and the standards are high. We genuinely like one another and love working here. People share discoveries, challenge each other's thinking, and step in to help, so the bar is high and so is the support around you.

About the work
Barrl is working with a travel management company that serves high-profile clients. Discretion and accuracy aren't nice-to-haves here. An error is visible immediately and expensive.
At any given time you'll own the outcome of two or three initiatives for them. Each one arrives as a business problem and leaves as something their team uses every day.
We're measured on results, not activity. An initiative counts when it's in production and we can show the client what changed.
What you'll do
Scope the work.
Take a vague business goal and turn it into something with a boundary, a sequence, and a definition of done. Push back when the ask doesn't match the problem.
Ship it.
Not a prototype, not a demo. Something the client's staff open on Monday morning and keep using.
Prove it worked.
Every initiative carries a number: hours saved, error rate, turnaround time, revenue touched. You set it before you build, instrument it as you go, and report it after. If you can't measure it, you haven't finished scoping it.
Work directly with the client.
Talk to their staff, run the demos, send the updates, manage expectations. You own the relationship on your initiatives.
Know when AI isn't the answer.
A lot of this work is AI-shaped. Some of it is a form, a database, and a clear owner. Knowing the difference, and being willing to say so, is a big part of the value.
Move on.
Ship, hand off cleanly, pick up the next thing. You'll be in an unfamiliar part of the business every few months.
First 90 days
30:
You understand the client's business well enough to have an opinion about what's worth building.
60:
One initiative in production, in daily use, with a number attached.
90:
You're scoping the next one yourself and the client comes to you directly.
What we're looking for
You've delivered for a business other than your own.
Agency, consulting, internal tools, freelance. Anywhere you had to learn someone else's process and hand back something that held up in production.
You finish.
Your track record is things running in the wild, not pilots that stalled at 80%.
You can point to outcomes.
Not "I built X" but "I built X and it cut Y by Z." If you've never worked that way, this will be uncomfortable.
You have real data skills.
SQL at minimum. You can get to the data, join it, and build the measurement yourself. Reading someone else's dashboard isn't the bar, and spreadsheets alone won't cut it.
You're precise.
This client's work doesn't tolerate approximation, and neither does a system that automates it. You test the edges before you ship.
You're discreet.
You'll have visibility into a sensitive book of business.
You learn unfamiliar domains fast.
You'll be handed a process you've never seen and expected to be useful within a week.
You're good in front of clients.
Comfortable saying "that'll take longer than you think" and "I don't think you actually want that."
What this isn't
Not a heads-down engineering role.
Expect to spend as much time with the client's staff as in the build.
Not an advisory role.
No decks, no recommendations you don't have to implement yourself.
Not an R&D role.
Proofs of concept are a step, never a deliverable. A PoC that doesn't reach production didn't happen.
Not a role with scaffolding.

Lodestar's mission is to develop the first "Protect and Defend" capability for high-value space assets in orbit. Our flagship product
MITHRIL
is our hardware-agnostic, AI-enabled autonomy software suite that enables us to augment any off-the-shelf spacecraft with the ability to autonomously detect, characterise, and reversibly neutralise orbital threats. By building on the proven space heritage of our best-in-class satellite-bus partners and fully integrating
MITHRIL
into single unified platform, we deliver an end-to-end, autonomous in-space bodyguarding service.

At Lodestar, as a
Software Engineer: State Estimation & Prediction
, you'll be leading the development of our state estimation and prediction models at the core of Lodestar's flagship product,
MITHRIL
. You'll be focusing on researching and developing algorithms that fuse probabilistic estimation with machine learning to track targets, predict trajectories and assess intent.
We proudly have an "extreme ownership" oriented engineering culture.

Design and implement Lodestar's core state estimation and prediction architecture for autonomous spacecraft operations

Familiarity with trajectory modeling, multi-body dynamics, or orbital mechanics

Track record implementing state estimation pipelines in real-time or safety-critical systems

Familiarity with sensor fusion techniques (e.g., combining radar, optical, and inertial data)

Why MOOV exists
Students walk into their buildings, hallways, and classrooms completely unaccounted for. As recent-ish public schoolers, we know the drill: put a backpack on, look the part, blend into the crowd. Teachers took attendance manually. They gave us blocks of wood and tissue boxes for hall passes. Finding one student meant logging into an attendance portal, calling into a classroom, and hoping. We also know what it's like to hear about a school shooting and start texting friends, wondering if you'll get a reply.
MOOV is our hope to make schools safer and seamless. It's an entirely new category in education technology: a student movement OS.
You cannot take one step into a MOOV school without noticing our impact. Anyone entering the building, a classroom, a bathroom, or a common area moves with MOOV. We are changing the culture of schools: from manual tasks, afterthought safety, and declining attendance, to automated attendance, accountability increased 10,000x (yes, that's a real number), and students earning points for getting to class early.
A principal at one of the biggest high schools in America was asked what would happen if MOOV were removed. He said his school could not function. Security Directors have said verbatim that MOOV "is a need, not a want."
We grew 252% last year
, and we're breaking into some of the country's biggest districts, all without a sales team.
Our mission is a relentless pursuit to reshape the schools that shaped us: saving time and saving lives.
The job
MOOV is hardware and software in the same product. A student taps a card in a classroom in California. A few hundred milliseconds later, an attendance record has to be right, a hall pass has to start counting, and an administrator's dashboard has to reflect it. When it's wrong, someone is wandering in a hallway and nobody can say where.
This role is mostly backend. The interesting problems at MOOV are underneath the screen: the ingestion path that takes tap events off thousands of devices, the sync layer that reconciles them against student information systems that were not designed to be integrated with, the provisioning and fleet health of hardware sitting in buildings we don't control. Front-end work exists, and you'll do some of it. It is not why we're hiring you.
Engineering at MOOV has been deliberately small, which means the scope in front of you is enormous: entire surfaces of this system are unclaimed, and you will own them from your first month rather than your third year. You report to Kevin, and you build alongside him.
Own backend surfaces outright.
The SIS integration layer, the event pipeline, or device provisioning and fleet health. Yours end to end, not yours to assist on. By month three Kevin should not be reviewing your work line by line, because he doesn't need to.
Make the tap path fast and correct
at real school-day volume, with roster data as it actually arrives: duplicate IDs, three date formats in one file, a district that renamed every room over the summer. The messy rows are not an edge case. They are the job.
Keep the fleet honest.
Readers, kiosks, and handhelds sit in buildings, on networks we didn't configure, 2,500 miles away. You'll care about what a device does when the Wi-Fi drops for six hours, and you'll be able to tell the difference between a firmware problem, a network problem, and a school that moved the Reader.
Be further out on AI than Kevin is
, and he is already out there. We want the person who shows up with the thing he hasn't seen yet: a better harness, an agent setup that actually holds up against a real codebase instead of a demo. If your answer to "what's changed in the last month" is what everyone else's answer is, you're not the hire.
And be able to do all of it with the tools switched off.
AI is how fast you go. It is not how you think. We will sit you in front of an unfamiliar system with no assistance and expect you to read it, find the thing that's wrong, and write the correct fix. Anyone who can only operate through a model is a liability here.
What you're walking into
We'd rather you hear this from us than find it in week one.
This is a young engineering organization and you are early in it. Decisions a larger company made five years ago have not been made here yet: how we test, how we review, what deploys look like as the team grows. You'll be in the room for those, and sometimes you'll be the one who makes them. If you want a system where all of that is settled, this is the wrong job.
The product is live, renewing, and running in districts every school day. What it hasn't been is built by more than a handful of people.
How we'll both know it worked
By week two:
you've shipped to production. Something small and real, in front of users, without anyone holding your hand through the deploy.
By month three:
you own a surface outright. You've taken something that only worked because someone knew how to hold it and made it work on its own.
By month six:
you've made the codebase easier for the next engineer and can point at exactly what. You've killed at least one whole category of support ticket with a product change. MOOV is shipping more per week than it was the day you started, and a meaningful share of that is yours.
This is a fast-track role.
We check in formally every 30 days, and the honest ceiling on this seat is leading engineering at MOOV. We promote execution, quickly, and we'd rather build our leadership team out of people who earned it here.
Who you are
You're better than us.
We don't have to push you; you push us. You're asking us to keep up.
You care deeply.
Not about "the platform" in the abstract, but about whether a specific kid in a specific hallway is accounted for.
You ship.
1-3 years shipping software professionally, or a shorter track record with unusually strong evidence of finished things in front of real users. Side projects count. Coursework doesn't.
You're high agency.

About FSU
We're building an AI-native applied learning platform: a 3D simulation engine that converts any syllabus or training doc into immersive, decision-based career simulations. Fortnite-meets-LinkedIn for education. Under the hood, FSU is a measurement system that happens to run as a game. Every decision a learner makes inside a sim becomes scored, traceable evidence of what they can actually do, and that evidence rolls up into the FSU Career Profile: a new kind of resume, built from behavior, not test scores.
We are live in real classrooms right now, with real professors and real students depending on the platform on a real semester schedule.
The Role
We're hiring a Forward-Deployed Engineer to be the technical front line between our customers and our codebase.
Today, support, triage, prod fixes, and professor onboarding get handled ad hoc by core engineering. That interrupts feature work and leaves no single person accountable for the customer's technical experience. This role consolidates all of it into one owner, spanning all three of our repos: the Unity simulation client, the platform backend (React/FastAPI), and the ML backend (Flask/Mongo).
You will be on calls with professors and in the codebase the same afternoon. You reproduce the problem, pull the session data, decide what it actually is, fix it if it's yours to fix, and write a crisp ticket if it isn't. Then you close the loop with the customer: here's what happened, here's the fix, you're set.
This is not a ticket-queue job. It's the role that turns customer pain into product signal, and it is one of the highest-leverage seats at the company because you see every failure mode before anyone else does.
What You'll Own
The bug pipeline, end to end.
Single owner of intake, triage, resolution, and closure. Reproduce, classify severity, deduplicate, track status, keep reporters updated. Nothing goes silent.
Triage and reproduction.
Pull the relevant logs and session data and classify root cause before fixing or routing. This is the judgment step that determines everything downstream.
Minor fixes across three repos.
Small issues you fix directly, in Unity/C#, React/FastAPI, or Flask/Mongo. Anything deeper becomes a well-scoped ticket with repro steps, impact, and a proposed direction, routed to the right owner.
Professor onboarding and course setup.
Class configuration, roster issues, sim and course assignment, and the setup problems that aren't bugs but still block a customer. This is the bulk of real support volume.
Prod data operations.
Careful production data work: grade corrections, content and assignment changes, migrations. Backup first, always, inside the guardrails below.
Post-deploy verification.
Smoke test every release end to end, including launching a live sim, so breakage gets caught here and not by a professor mid-class.
Proactive monitoring.
Watch health and alerts for outages and degradations across memory, sessions, and third-party services, and raise them before they show up as customer reports.
Runbooks and knowledge base.
Turn recurring issues into docs and self-serve guides so the same problem doesn't get re-diagnosed five times, and so professors can resolve common things themselves.
Voice of the customer.
Spot patterns across bug reports and surface them to product and engineering as prioritized signal, with the underlying cause attached.

Our Company Values
Our four values aren't aspirational. They translate into concrete operating tenets that shape how we make decisions every day.
Beat Yesterday.
We re-evaluate our own toolkit every quarter, because the workflows that made you effective three months ago may already be outdated. GIGR is building Playad, an AI agent team for marketing.

Most companies separate Growth, Customer Success, Marketing, Product, and Engineering.

A customer may struggle during onboarding. The right users may not understand our value quickly enough. A useful feature may remain undiscovered. A promising campaign may generate attention without creating lasting value.
Your job is to notice these gaps—and close them.

Mearas builds ATHENA, a software-defined, drive-by-wire electric ground vehicle that a person can drive, an operator can run remotely, or a third-party autonomy stack can host — one chassis for all three. ATHENA has been through a U.S. Army field assessment, we hold an executed CRADA with the Army's Ground Vehicle Systems Center, and USSOCOM has asked for an in-person technical demonstration this fall. Vehicle integration — the software that talks to propulsion, steering, and braking over CAN, plus telemetry and logging. Off-the-shelf components; your code is the glue that makes them one vehicle.

Operator tooling — the remote station, visualization, replay, and the data that proves what the vehicle did during a demonstration.
Not the job: electrical design, harnessing, VCU hardware, or autonomy research. Those have owners; you'll work next to them.

If you already work this way and can show us something you shipped, you're the profile.

Python, some C++, and comfort on Linux. CAN bus experience is a plus; the willingness to learn it in a month is required.
Enough networking to reason about a video stream over a bad link.
A safety-first instinct and the honesty to say "I don't know" before the vehicle moves.

Strayos builds visual AI technology for mining and heavy-industry operations. Our platform transforms data from drones, cameras, LiDAR, field sensors, equipment, and geospatial systems into accurate digital twins and decision intelligence across the mine-to-mill value chain.
We work on problems where AI must perform beyond a controlled laboratory environment. Data is large, multimodal, spatial, imperfect, and collected under changing field conditions. The systems we build must be accurate, explainable, production-ready, and useful to engineers and operators making consequential decisions.
The Opportunity
We are looking for an
AI Engineer — Visual, Agentic & Geospatial AI
to help build the next generation of Strayos intelligence products. This role sits at the intersection of
Visual Language Models, computer vision, agentic AI, 3D digital twins, geospatial computing, and Physical AI datasets
.
You will develop AI systems that can understand imagery, video, maps, point clouds, site models, documents, and operational data; reason across these inputs; call the appropriate vision and geospatial tools; and return trustworthy, actionable results. You will also help create the datasets, evaluation systems, and production infrastructure required to make these capabilities reliable in real-world industrial environments.
This is an applied engineering role for someone who enjoys moving between research, data, software, and product—and who measures success by what works for customers in production.
What You Will Do
Visual LLMs and multimodal AI :
Adapt, fine-tune, evaluate, and deploy vision-language and multimodal foundation models for visual question answering, grounding, classification, detection, segmentation, change analysis, report generation, and spatial reasoning
Agentic computer vision :
Create agents that plan multi-step visual workflows, select and call computer-vision or geospatial tools, maintain context, verify intermediate outputs, quantify uncertainty, and involve a human when confidence is insufficient.
Digital-twin intelligence :
Develop models and algorithms that reason over orthomosaics, terrain and surface models, meshes, point clouds, LiDAR, raster and vector layers, and time-series site captures
Physical AI datasets :
Design data-collection and labeling strategies for models grounded in real sites, sensors, machines, and environmental conditions. Establish annotation ontologies, quality controls, lineage, versioning, privacy and safety practices, and representative evaluation sets.
Production AI systems :
Build modular training and inference pipelines, APIs, batch and streaming workflows, model registries, observability, rollback paths, and cloud or edge deployment strategies. Optimize latency, memory, throughput, reliability, and cost without compromising measurable quality.
What You Will Bring
Applied AI delivery :
You have built and shipped computer-vision, multimodal, or Visual LLM systems beyond prototypes, and you can explain how quality was measured after deployment
Modern model development :
You are highly proficient in Python and modern deep-learning frameworks, especially PyTorch. You understand transformers, vision-language models, multimodal embeddings, model adaptation, retrieval, structured outputs, tool use, and systematic evaluation.
Computer vision :
You have practical experience in several areas such as detection, segmentation, tracking, metric learning, OCR, multimodal fusion, image and video understanding, or 2D/3D reconstruction.
3D and geospatial data :
You have worked with one or more spatial representations such as point clouds, meshes, LiDAR, orthophotos, digital elevation or surface models, raster and vector layers, coordinate systems, or spatial databases.
Technical foundations :
You bring strong applied problem-solving skills in linear algebra, probability and statistics, optimization, and 2D/3D geometry and working knowledge on RGB, video, thermal, multispectral or hyperspectral cameras, LiDAR, GNSS/IMU, IoT sensors, drones, scanners, or heavy equipment.
What Success Looks Like
Within your first year, you will have shipped customer-facing multimodal or agentic AI capabilities; established measurable evaluation baselines; improved the quality, coverage, and reuse of Physical AI datasets; and contributed reusable components that accelerate future Strayos products. You will be trusted to move from an ambiguous field problem to a well-scoped technical approach, a validated model, and a monitored production system.
Why Join Strayos
You will work on AI problems that connect digital intelligence to the physical world. The role offers the opportunity to combine modern foundation models with computer vision, 3D geometry, geospatial data, digital twins, and industrial domain expertise—and to see that work influence real operational decisions.
You will have meaningful ownership across the full AI lifecycle: problem definition, data strategy, research, evaluation, production deployment, and continuous improvement. You will work with a collaborative, globally distributed team that values practical innovation, technical rigor, and customer impact.

Integrate motors, actuators, encoders, and sensors into the machine and support commissioning of integrated hardware
Develop test fixtures and scripts, collect data, investigate electrical and firmware failures, and feed findings into the next design iteration

Experience in robotics, industrial automation, aerospace, automotive, heavy machinery, construction equipment, or similarly complex hardware systems is particularly relevant

Our sensors output detections, tracks, and imagery products at high rates, and users need to work with that output in real time, often on limited hardware and unreliable networks. You will build the web applications they use, along with the integrations that carry our output into the systems they already run, including TAK and customer C2 and autonomy platforms. You will work with radar and embedded engineers on the data contracts behind the product and with end users on the workflows in front of it.

Design and build production web applications for real-time RF output visualization, including live detections and tracks, spectrogram displays, geospatial overlays, and post-mission playback and review

Engineer for performance at high data rates: streaming ingest, efficient rendering, memory discipline, and smooth interaction on modest field hardware
Define and shape the APIs and data contracts between the frontend and our embedded and backend systems, in partnership with the teams that build them
Build and maintain integrations that deliver SoloPulse detections and tracks into the systems our users already operate, including TAK (ATAK, WinTAK, iTAK, and TAK Server) over Cursor on Target, along with customer C2, autonomy, and ISR platforms

Partner with integrators and government end users during integration events and demonstrations, and turn what breaks in those environments into durable product improvements
Work directly with operators, test engineers, and customers to translate real workflows into features, and validate that what shipped actually works for them
Establish frontend fundamentals as the product grows, including component architecture, testing, build and release tooling, telemetry, and error reporting
Support field testing and deployments, including on-site debugging of the full stack from sensor to screen
Collaborate with a broad range of cross-functional teams including radar, embedded software, hardware, program management, and senior leadership
Qualifications
At least a bachelor's degree in computer science, engineering, or other technical field, or equivalent practical experience
6+ years of professional frontend application development experience, preferably on data-intensive, visualization-heavy, or mapping products
Expert-level proficiency in JavaScript, TypeScript, and React

Demonstrated track record of shipping production interfaces that users depend on, and owning changes and maintenance after launch
Working knowledge of backend web services and API design; comfortable reading and contributing to the services your interfaces consume
Must be eligible to obtain and maintain a U.S. TS clearance
Nice-to-Have
Experience with browser graphics programming (WebGL, WebGPU, Canvas, or a rendering library built on them) for large or continuously updating datasets
Experience with real-time, high-performance DSP or sensor data visualization (waterfall displays, spectrograms, radar or sonar imagery)
Experience with mapping and geospatial visualization stacks (Mapbox GL, deck.gl, Cesium, or similar)
Hands-on experience with the TAK ecosystem: ATAK/WinTAK plugin development, TAK Server deployment or federation, Cursor on Target message design, or data package workflows
Familiarity with interoperability and messaging standards used across defense and autonomy systems, such as STANAG 4676, ASTERIX, MISB/KLV, KML and GeoJSON, MQTT, ROS 2, or MAVLink
Experience with Dart and Flutter, or a comparable cross-platform framework, for building tablet and handheld clients that run alongside our web applications in the field
Experience with browser streaming technologies (WebSockets, WebRTC, WebTransport) and binary protocols such as Protobuf or FlatBuffers
Experience with multi-threaded browser development using Web Workers, WASM, or SharedArrayBuffer
Experience developing and maintaining reusable TypeScript libraries or internal design systems
Experience building software for defense, aerospace, autonomy, or other operational environments

Consumer privacy is top of mind in today’s advertising industry. Regulators worldwide are now forcing browser and other platform vendors to build in consumer privacy from the ground up.
